title: Ekalavya and the clay teacher
hookLine: turned away by Drona, Ekalavya practices before a clay Drona until his skill passes Arjuna's
carry: samyama: the three, held on one thing
tomorrow: The king and the palanquin bearer

cards: Drona, the archery teacher from yesterday, gets a visitor. Ekalavya, son of a Nishada chief from the forest, asks to be his student. Drona turns him away; in the Mahabharata it's because of the people he was born into.
Ekalavya bows at Drona's feet anyway and goes back into the forest. There he shapes a Drona out of clay, sets it up, and treats it as his teacher.
Every day he bows to it and practices before it: the same image, the same bow, the same target, month after month.

teach.b: One day the royal princes go hunting, and their dog runs barking at a dark stranger in the woods. Before it can close its mouth, seven arrows fill it, and the dog runs back to the princes. They're amazed.
Arjuna is upset: Drona had promised no student would ever surpass him. So Drona goes into the forest. Who is your teacher?
You are, says Ekalavya. Then, says Drona, I want my fee: your right thumb. Ekalavya cuts it off and gives it without a word, and after that his shooting is never as swift.
Many Hindus today hear this as a wrong done to a boy shut out for his birth, and the boy they remember as the model student is Ekalavya.

teach.h: SAMYAMA: THE THREE ON ONE THING.
teach.b: Patanjali's word for how he learned is samyama. Sutra 3.4: concentration, meditation and absorption, all three on one object, together. Sam, together; yama, holding.
Sutra 3.5: mastered, the light of insight, prajna, shines. Sutra 3.6: it's applied in stages.
The classical commentary adds: yoga is known by yoga. No one stood beside Ekalavya; the practice itself taught him the next step.

teach.h: EVEN THESE ARE OUTER TO THE SEEDLESS.
teach.b: Then 3.8, the humbling line: even these three are outer, compared with the seedless samadhi of book one.

One way to read the story with it: a skill can be taken in a moment; a devotion can't. It's also why many Hindus keep one mantra, one form of God, one teacher, for a lifetime, not swapped for something new each week.
Depth comes from staying with one thing until it opens.

how: Many Hindus keep one mantra, one form of God or one teacher for life, and students of music and dance often bow to their guru, or the guru's picture, before practice; teachers of the Yoga Sutras present samyama as the three inner limbs held together on one object, learned gradually over years, and stress that its fruits are not the goal.

o: wisdom's light, shining when samyama is mastered
the breath that rises in deep meditation
a mantra repeated to steady a restless mind

games.q: the three together — tap the pairs.

s: samyama is a ninth limb added after samadhi
3.4: it's the three inner limbs together on one object.
Ekalavya learned with no teacher beside him, before a clay image
the practice itself carried him, stage by stage.
the Yoga Sutras call samyama the final goal
3.8: even these three are outer compared with seedless samadhi.

games.q: a meditation app gives you a new practice every day. nani has said one mantra for sixty years. by sutra 3.6, which way does samyama deepen?
o: by switching: variety keeps the mind fresh.
by staying with one, stage by stage.
it doesn't deepen; it works or it doesn't.
games.why: 3.6: samyama is applied in stages, and the commentary says yoga is known by yoga. ekalavya practiced before the same clay image, day after day.

practice: If you pray, choose one name of God, the one your family uses, or a mantra you already know, and repeat it softly inside. If you don't, choose one word, or the breath at the nose.
Hold the mind there, and let the holding become a flow. Often the mind stays on the first strand, and that's the work. Keep the same one tomorrow.

wordCard.voice: Prajna, wisdom's light, which begins to shine when samyama is mastered: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object at once, the tool of book three.

orig.note: Sanskrit saṃyama: sam (together) plus yama (holding, restraint); dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi on one object.

carryVoice: Your line: samyama: the three, held on one thing. The same image, the same target, all the way down. That's day four sixty-six.
